common_name: Cardinal Bearded Iris (Historic 1919 Lavender-Rose and Raisin-Purple Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Cardinal is an early tetraploid English iris later used in American red-iris breeding, including as a parent of the 1929 Dykes Medal winner 'Dauntless'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in loose, well-drained soil in full sun. Cardinal was bred by English hybridizer Arthur J. Bliss from his influential blue-purple bitone 'Dominion' crossed with 'Trosuperba', and was introduced in 1919 before quickly crossing the Atlantic into American breeding programs. Despite its fiery name, the flower is a fragrant bitone with lavender-rose standards over velvety raisin-purple to prune-purple falls, carried on low, wide-branching stems, and it earned an Award of Merit from the Royal Horticultural Society in 1927 followed by a First Class Certificate in 1930. Its main legacy is as a breeding parent: crossed with Grace Sturtevant's 'Rose Madder', it produced Clarence Connell's 1929 Dykes Medal winner 'Dauntless', and it was also used in the Sass brothers' red-iris lines behind 'The Red Douglas'. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding old woody rhizomes.

common_name: Rose Madder Bearded Iris (Historic 1920 Argyle-Purple and Dahlia-Purple Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Rose Madder is a tall, strong-growing historic iris best known as the pollen parent of the 1929 Dykes Medal winner 'Dauntless'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil. Rose Madder was bred by pioneering American hybridizer Grace Sturtevant from a cross of ('Hector' x 'Shelford Chieftain') with itself, and was introduced in 1920, earning an Honorable Mention the same year. The flower carries argyle-purple standards with a darker margin over dark, velvety dahlia-purple falls on a tall, sturdy 40-inch stalk, a combination contemporary catalogs described as true rose-madder tones. Its chief claim to fame is as the pollen parent of Clarence Connell's garnet-red 'Dauntless', which went on to win the American Dykes Medal in 1929. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, keeping rhizomes shallow and in full sun.

common_name: Redwing Bearded Iris (Historic 1927 Sass Red-Toned Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Redwing is a Hans Sass red-toned blend from Nebraska's early red-iris breeding program, later used as a grandparent of the 1941 Dykes Medal winner 'The Red Douglas'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Redwing was bred by Hans P. Sass of Nebraska, originally noted among his seedlings as a 'Red Wonder' selection before being registered under the Redwing name and introduced in 1927, growing into a richly blended red bicolor with light brownish-vinaceous standards over dahlia-carmine falls on a 36-inch stalk. It came out of Sass's variegata-patterned seedlings crossed onto the Vilmorin violet bitone 'Alcazar', part of the family's long push toward true red bearded irises. Crossed with 'Cardinal' and then with 'Joycette', it became a grandparent of Jacob Sass's 1941 Dykes Medal winner 'The Red Douglas'. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Joycette Bearded Iris (Historic 1931 Red Self Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Joycette is a Jacob Sass red self later used as a parent of the 1941 Dykes Medal winner 'The Red Douglas'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Joycette was hybridized by Jacob Sass of Nebraska from a cross of 'King Tut' and 'Baldwin', registered in 1931 and introduced jointly with Kellogg in 1932, producing a neutral-red self with bordeaux-red falls on a well-branched, smooth-finished flower that earned an Honorable Mention in 1932 and an Award of Merit in 1936. Its pollen parent 'King Tut' gave the saturated red tone while 'Baldwin' contributed height and a flower of good size and substance. Joycette's own importance came as a parent: crossed with ('Redwing' x 'Cardinal'), it helped produce 'The Red Douglas', which won the American Dykes Medal in 1941, and Joycette itself was later inducted into the Iris Hall of Fame. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep plantings vigorous.

common_name: Crispette Bearded Iris (Historic 1954 Pearly Orchid Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Crispette is a Schreiner's orchid self later used as a parent of the 1963 Dykes Medal winner 'Amethyst Flame'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil. Crispette was bred by Robert Schreiner from a multi-generation Schreiner's Gardens breeding line and registered in 1954, producing a pearly orchid self with a glistening overtone of pink on a 36-inch stalk that blooms in late midseason. Although period photographs sometimes skewed its color toward rose, growers of the era described the true flower as a deep, glowing orchid rather than pink. Crossed with ('Lavanesque' x 'Pathfinder'), Crispette became a parent of Schreiner's 'Amethyst Flame', which went on to win the American Dykes Medal in 1963 and top the AIS popularity polls in 1964 and 1965. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, replanting only vigorous outer rhizomes.

common_name: Lavanesque Bearded Iris (Historic 1953 Orchid-Pink Bitone Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Lavanesque is a Schreiner's orchid-pink bitone later used as a parent of the 1963 Dykes Medal winner 'Amethyst Flame'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. Lavanesque was bred by Robert Schreiner and registered in 1953, producing a lavender bitone with light orchid-pink standards over darker orchid-pink falls and a lemon-yellow beard, on a tall 40-inch stalk blooming early to midseason. It earned an Honorable Mention in 1955 and an Award of Merit in 1959 in its own right. Crossed with 'Pathfinder' and then combined with 'Crispette', Lavanesque contributed to Schreiner's 'Amethyst Flame', the amethyst-orchid self that won the American Dykes Medal in 1963. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Pathfinder Bearded Iris (Historic 1948 Pink Blend Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; this Pathfinder is a 1948 pink-blend bearded iris later used as a parent of the 1963 Dykes Medal winner 'Amethyst Flame' (not to be confused with the unrelated Panicum virgatum switchgrass cultivar of the same name).

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in loose, well-drained soil. This Pathfinder was bred by Mrs. C. Whiting from a cross of 'Mirabelle' and 'Angelus' and registered in 1948, producing a big, wide-hafted pink blend with heavy substance and a glistening texture on a 36-inch stalk, leaning slightly toward lavender rather than true pink; it received an Honorable Mention the year it was introduced. Used as part of the ('Lavanesque' x 'Pathfinder') cross with Schreiner's 'Crispette', it became a grandparent of 'Amethyst Flame', the 1963 American Dykes Medal winner. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the oldest central rhizomes.

common_name: Epic Bearded Iris (Historic 1964 Powder-Blue Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Epic is a Sanford Babson powder-blue self later used as a parent of the 1974 Dykes Medal winner 'Shipshape'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Epic was bred by Sanford Babson from a cross of his seedling K97 with 'Fragrant Sapphire' and registered in the mid-1960s at his Melrose Gardens, producing a medium powder-blue self with an opalescent orchid flicker and wide, fluted petals on a 36-inch stalk, earning an Honorable Mention in 1966. Crossed with Neva Sexton's 'Pacific Panorama', Epic became a parent of Babson's own 'Shipshape', the massive medium-blue self that won the American Dykes Medal in 1974. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep plants flowering well.

common_name: Tom Johnson Bearded Iris (Dark Purple and Velvety Black Fragrant Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; 'Tom Johnson' is a fragrant dark purple-black Paul Black iris named for his Mid-America Iris Garden business partner and later used as a parent of the 2010 Dykes Medal winner 'Paul Black'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to sunlight in well-drained soil. The cultivar 'Tom Johnson' was hybridized by Paul Black from the cross 'Witches' Sabbath' x 'In Town' and registered in 1996, producing an early-blooming, ruffled flower with dark purple standards and style arms over velvety purple-black falls narrowly edged in dark purple, set off by red-orange beards and a slight spicy fragrance on a 35-inch stalk. Black named the introduction after Tom Johnson, his co-owner at Mid-America Iris Garden in Salem, Oregon. In a fitting turnabout, Johnson later used 'Tom Johnson' crossed with Keith Keppel's 'Star Fleet' to breed and name 'Paul Black' after his partner, and that iris won the American Dykes Medal in 2010. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep plantings vigorous.

common_name: Star Fleet Bearded Iris (Mulberry-and-Canterbury-Purple Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Star Fleet is a Keith Keppel bitone later used by Thomas Johnson as a parent of the 2010 Dykes Medal winner 'Paul Black'.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun. Star Fleet was bred by Keith Keppel from a complex multi-generation cross and registered in 1992, producing a late-midseason bloom with near mulberry-purple standards over canterbury-purple falls showing redder margins and dark rosy-brown haft suffusion, with beards shading from tomato-red to orange-vermilion and tipped lavender, on a 38-inch stalk; it earned an Honorable Mention in 1995. Thomas Johnson later crossed Star Fleet with his own 'Tom Johnson' to produce 'Paul Black', naming it for his Mid-America Iris Garden business partner, and that cross went on to win the American Dykes Medal in 2010. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Festive Azalea (White Purple-Red-Streaked Glenn Dale Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Festive is a large, spreading Glenn Dale Hybrid grown for its white flowers streaked and blotched with purplish red.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade, allowing plenty of room since this selection grows larger than most Glenn Dale cultivars. Festive was bred by Benjamin Yeo Morrison at the USDA's Glenn Dale Plant Introduction Station from a cross of the old Japanese clones 'Vittata Fortunei' and 'Ho Oden', producing a single, roughly 2.25-inch flower that reads white at a distance but carries fine purplish-red streaks and occasional bold blotches running the length of each petal. The shrub grows into a large, well-branched, semi-evergreen to evergreen mound that can reach 5 to 6 feet tall and wide at maturity, considerably bigger than many of its Glenn Dale siblings, and flowers in a single heavy spring flush. Water deeply during dry spells, keep the shallow root zone mulched, and prune only right after bloom since next year's buds set soon afterward.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture Cooperative Extension
